title: Fractal KV-Cache Archives: Lossless Symbolic Storage with In-Place Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Inference
event_hint: arXiv publication on KV cache compression archive format
problem: KV cache dominates memory cost of long-context autoregressive inference; once quantized to codebook indices, the resulting symbol stream needs storage that supports the access patterns of a growing cache (random access and append)
mechanism: Contractive iterated-map code (fractal archive) that serializes symbol sequences into low-dimensional real vectors, providing lossless storage with O(1) random access and O(1) amortized append, while simultaneously functioning as a search index for approximate substring queries

evidence.claim: Codec encoding runs in linear time at 0.68µs per character

evidence.condition: 10^6-character document, decoding only the span containing the target
token-by-token append, re-walking only from last stored anchor

evidence.claim: Per-head hybrid bit-asymmetric RVQ (K×4, V×2) achieves 36x compression vs fp16 at +11.2% perplexity cost
Archive-based search index achieves 1.00 recall for approximate substring queries
evidence.condition: Nearest-neighbor distance thresholding on stored vectors, query encoded from origin

evaluation_context: GPT-2 (124M parameters) on The Time Machine (Project Gutenberg public domain text), 1024-token context windows, 4 attention sinks + 32 recent tokens kept exact, remainder archived. Perplexity measured token-by-token, baseline perplexity 35.97. Codebooks trained by k-means on disjoint span of same book. All experiments run on single laptop CPU within minutes. Code released at github.com/eighteight/fractal-kv.
limitations: Evaluated only on GPT-2 (124M) - not validated on production-scale models. Archive format itself produces size comparable to bit-packing; compression ratio comes from upstream vector quantizer. Lossy regime (truncated points) forfeits random access and in-place search properties. Multi-span truncation damages recent context as much as distant context, requiring explicit exact-window policy rather than free recency gradient. Per-head codebooks trained per corpus rather than amortized - a deployable system would need corpus-independent or online codebooks. Serialization ties rather than beats byte-oriented coders on raw size; advantage is access pattern, not compression ratio. Study does not benchmark against concurrent random-access KV quantizers such as FibQuant.
project_relevance: Directly addresses KV cache compression (36x vs fp16) which reduces transfer bytes for cross-region KV cache scenarios. Archive format's O(1) random access enables efficient retrieval patterns in distributed cache settings. Search index capability (1.00 recall) could enable content-based routing/prefetching across regions. Key/value asymmetry insight could inform selective compression strategies for transfer optimization. However, corpus-specific codebook training and lack of production-scale evaluation limit direct deployment readiness.
source_notes: Code and scripts released at https://github.com/eighteight/fractal-kv

evidence_gaps.question: What is the end-to-end bandwidth reduction and transfer time impact for cross-region KV cache deployment?
How does this approach scale to production-scale models (hundreds of kilobytes per token) and what are the consistency/maintenance overheads?
What are the incremental encoding/update patterns for streaming contexts and partial cache invalidation?
